papers.title_in_file: General parameter-shift rules for quantum gradients
papers.version_note: arXiv:2107.12390v3, 22 Mar 2022, as accepted in Quantum 2022-03-18. The text layer holds the paper twice (the arXiv layout, then a second two-column copy); the first copy was read in full and the second was not needed. The text layer carries no page-break characters; the 26 page footers of the first copy gave the page count.
papers.what_it_is: A paper that derives general parameter-shift rules and full function reconstructions for variational quantum circuits from the finite Fourier-series form of their cost functions, with resource analyses for gradients, Hessians and the metric tensor, and applications to QAOA, Rotosolve and quantum analytic descent.

existing.note: The saving is narrower than the abstract's wording. Sec. 5.1 states it as a constant prefactor (the gradient cost halved), and an improvement of at least O(N) only for gradient and Hessian together. It needs an upper bound on the largest eigenvalue of the problem Hamiltonian, since the frequencies are not known in advance. Sec. 3.5.2 states that in shot count the general rule shows no general advantage, so the saving holds for the number of unique circuits. The quote 'cut in half' is in Sec. 5.1, not the abstract.
existing.value: The authors report, for MaxCut QAOA circuits, that the generalized parameter-shift rule gives a constant prefactor improvement for the gradient and an improvement of at least O(N ) for gradient and Hessian together, as counted in circuit evaluations and with an upper bound on the largest eigenvalue; they state that the general rule does not show lower shot requirements in general.
quotes: we find the generalized parametershift rule to offer a constant prefactor improvement when computing the gradient and an improvement of at least O(N ) when computing both the gradient and the Hessian.
the general parameter-shift rule does not show lower shot requirements in general
existing.certainty_reason: A resource count from the paper's own scaling table and sampled graphs (N at most 20 in the figure), one study.
existing.reader_inference: The abstract's word 'significantly' is a loose summary of a constant-factor saving for the gradient.

assertions.value: The paper considers a gate defined by a Hermitian generator G and parametrized by a single parameter x, and shows that the expectation value of an observable in the state it prepares is a finite-term Fourier series (a trigonometric polynomial) in x, with frequencies given by the differences of the generator's eigenvalues.
quotes: Let us first consider the expectation value for a general gate U (x) = exp(ixG), defined by a Hermitian generator G and parametrized by a single parameter x.
with frequencies given by the differences
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's definition of its setting, Section 2.1, which all later results use.

assertions.value: The authors state that the full functional form of E(x) can be obtained from a finite number of evaluations of E(x), from which derivatives of arbitrary order can be computed.
quotes: we can obtain the full functional form of E(x) from a finite number of evaluations of E(x), from which we can compute arbitrary order derivatives.
assertions.certainty_reason: A statement of the core observation; the proofs are in Sec. 3 and App. A.

assertions.value: The paper states that, for equidistant integer frequencies, the function E(x) is determined by computing 2R + 1 coefficients, and that the full function can be obtained at the price of 2R + 1 evaluations.
quotes: We can thus determine the function by computing the 2R + 1 coefficients
the full function can be obtained at the price of 2R + 1 evaluations
assertions.certainty_reason: The statement is quoted; the conditions (equidistant frequencies rescaled to integers) are set in the Section 3 preface, not in these quotes.

assertions.value: The paper states that the odd part of E can be determined from evaluations at R distinct points, which takes 2R evaluations of E, saving one evaluation compared with the general case, and that the saved evaluation of E at zero is evaluated in many applications anyway, so the saving has no significant impact in effect.
quotes: The coefficients in Eodd can be determined by evaluating Eodd at R distinct points
Thus, the odd part of E can be completely determined with 2R evaluations of E, saving one evaluation compared to the general case.
Note however that the saved E(0) evaluation is evaluated regardless in many applications, and may be used to recover the full reconstruction
assertions.certainty_reason: A counting argument in Section 3.2 with its condition (R distinct points, equidistant integer frequencies) stated in the section.

assertions.value: The paper states that determining the even part of E takes 2R + 1 evaluations for arbitrary frequencies, but that when the frequencies are integers periodicity reduces this to 2R evaluations of E, saving one evaluation over the general case.
quotes: Determining Eeven(x) requires R + 1 evaluations of Eeven, which leads to 2R + 1 evaluations of E for arbitrary frequencies.
However, in the case where Ω are integers, R + 1 evaluations of Eeven can be obtained
Thus, in this case 2R evaluations of E(x) suffice to determine its even part, saving one evaluation over the general case.
assertions.certainty_reason: The statement and its integer-frequency condition are quoted from Section 3.3.

assertions.value: The authors state that the general first- and second-order shift rules use evenly spaced points, use different evaluation points for the first and second derivatives with 2R evaluations for each, and reduce to the known two-term and four-term rules for R = 1 and R = 2, respectively.
quotes: this result reduces to the known two-term (Eq. (7)) and four-term (Eq. (8)) parameter-shift rules for R = 1 and R = 2, respectively
We again note that the formulas above use different evaluation points for the first and second derivatives (2R evaluations for each derivative).
assertions.certainty_reason: The explicit formulas (Eqs. 24 and 25) are garbled in the text layer, so the theorem statements are not quoted; the derivation is in App. A.1.

assertions.value: The paper defines two resource measures for comparing shift rules: the number of distinct circuits to be evaluated, Neval, and the overall number N of measurements (shots), irrespective of the number of unique circuits.
quotes: the number of distinct circuits that need to be evaluated to obtain all terms of a shift rule, Neval.
Secondly, we consider the overall number N of measurements
irrespective of the number of unique circuits they are distributed across.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own definitions, Section 2.3.

assertions.value: The authors state that, for the shot-count analysis, they approximate the one-shot variance of the cost function as constant across its domain, and that they are forced to make this potentially very rough approximation because the variance cannot in general be computed analytically.
quotes: we approximate the physical (one-shot) variance σ2 of the cost function E to be constant across its domain
As it is impossible in general to compute σ2 analytically, we are forced to make this potentially very rough approximation.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states the assumption and its roughness in Section 2.3.

assertions.value: The authors state that they mostly use the number of unique circuits to compare shift rules, because it is more accessible, does not rely on the constant-variance assumption, and the coefficients needed for the shot count are not known analytically in most general cases; they claim that hardware is typically billed and queued per unique circuit, so this number often dictates financial and time cost.
quotes: In this work we will mostly use Neval to compare the requirements of different parameter-shift rules as it is more accessible
quantum hardware devices are typically billed and queued per unique circuit, and as a result Neval often dictates both the financial and time cost.
assertions.certainty_reason: The billing statement is a claim about cloud services without a cited source in this passage.

assertions.value: The paper states that a decomposition into P gates that depend on x needs 2P unique circuit evaluations for the first derivative, so the general parameter-shift rule is cheaper if R < P, and that obtaining the second derivative by decomposition requires 2P squared minus P plus 1 evaluations (printed 2P2−P+1), significantly more than the 2R evaluations of the general rule.
quotes: this approach requires 2P unique circuit evaluations; as a result, the general parameter-shift rule is cheaper if R < P.
which requires 2P2−P+1 evaluations, including E(0), and thus is significantly more expensive than the 2R evaluations for the general parameter-shift rule.
assertions.certainty_reason: A counting result stated in Section 3.5.1 with its setting (P gates in the decomposition, each with the two-term rule).

assertions.value: The authors state that a decomposition-based approach would demand a full multivariate reconstruction over all P parametrized elementary gates to obtain the dependence on x, requiring O(2P) evaluations (exponent printed flat in the text layer), whereas the general approach computes the dependence in 2R + 1 evaluations and is the only method for which the univariate reconstruction is viable.
quotes: requiring O(2P ) evaluations.
The approach shown here allows us to compute the dependence in 2R + 1 evaluations and thus is the only method for which the univariate reconstruction is viable.
assertions.certainty_reason: The exclusivity claim is stated in a sentence without a proof of optimality.
assertions.reader_inference: The text layer printed the exponent flat, so 'two to the power P' is the reader's reading of O(2P).

assertions.value: The paper reports that the shot budgets of the general shift rule and of the decomposition approach are equal at P = R, so for both the first and second derivative the general rule does not show lower shot requirements in general, unlike its smaller number of unique circuits for the second derivative; the authors state that the comparison depends on the chosen resource measure.
quotes: Comparing with NgenPS, 1 and NgenPS, 2 above, we see that the shot budgets are equal at P = R.

the general parameter-shift rule does not show lower shot requirements in general, in contrast to the previous analysis that showed a significantly smaller number of unique circuits for the second derivative.
This shows that the comparison of recipes for gradients and higherorder derivatives crucially depends on the chosen resource measure.
assertions.certainty_reason: A derived comparison under the stated constant-variance assumption of Section 2.3 and equidistant shifts; the coefficient norms are derived in App. A.4.
assertions.reader_inference: The result holds under the paper's constant one-shot-variance approximation, which the paper calls potentially very rough.

assertions.value: The authors state that the stochastic parameter-shift rule combined with the generalized shift rule allows differentiating any unitary with equidistant frequencies, including multi-parameter gates because the extra operator may contain terms that depend on other variational parameters, and that with the rule for arbitrary frequencies it covers any quantum gate whose frequencies are known.
quotes: The stochastic parameter-shift rule in combination with the generalized shift rule in Eq. (24) allows for the differentiation of any unitary with equidistant frequencies.
As F in UF (x) above is allowed to contain terms that depend on other variational parameters, this includes multi-parameter gates in particular.
allows us to compute the derivative of any quantum gate as long as the frequencies of UF =0(x) are known.
assertions.certainty_reason: The rule (Eq. 33) is garbled in the text layer so its statement is not quoted; the derivation is in App. C.

assertions.value: The paper attributes the original stochastic parameter-shift rule to Ref. [39], for gates of a given form built from a Hermitian generator G with eigenvalues of plus and minus one and another Hermitian operator F that may not commute with G.
quotes: In Ref. [39], the authors derive the stochastic parameter-shift rule for gates of the form
G is a Hermitian operator with eigenvalues ±1 (so that G2 = 1), e.g., a Pauli word.
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the paper attributes to other work.

assertions.value: The authors state that each diagonal entry of the Hessian needs 2Rk evaluations since it is the second derivative of a univariate restriction of E, and that for equidistant frequencies the diagonal shift rule for an off-diagonal entry requires 2(Rk + Rm) − 1 evaluations once the diagonal is known.
quotes: 2Rk evaluations are sufficient as it is the second derivative of a univariate restriction of E
the diagonal shift rule for Hkm requires 2(Rk + Rm) − 1 evaluations, assuming the diagonal and thus E(x0) to be known already.
assertions.certainty_reason: A counting result stated with its conditions (equidistant frequencies, diagonal and E(x0) known) in Sections 4.1 and 4.2.1.

assertions.value: The paper states that the restriction of E along a simultaneous shift of two parameters is again a Fourier series with Rkm = Rk + Rm equidistant frequencies, which gives the Hessian off-diagonal entries via the diagonal shift rule.
quotes: We show in App. A.2 that E(km) again is a Fourier series of x with Rkm = Rk + Rm equidistant frequencies.
In case of integer-valued frequencies, there are Rkm = Rk + Rm such positive frequencies, namely all integers in [Rk + Rm].
assertions.certainty_reason: A derived statement with its condition (integer-valued frequencies) quoted from App. A.2.

assertions.value: The authors state that the repeated general shift rule requires strictly more circuit evaluations than the diagonal shift rule for the Hessian, and that the best choice between the diagonal rule and decomposition depends on Rk,m and Pk,m.
quotes: The repeated general shift rule requires strictly more circuit evaluations than the diagonal shift rule
the optimal approach depends on Rk,m and Pk,m
assertions.certainty_reason: The inequality (Eq. 39) is garbled in the text layer, so its statement is not quoted.

assertions.value: The authors state that the diagonal shift rule for the Hessian is significantly less efficient than repeating the general parameter-shift rule if the shot count is the relevant resource measure, while its number of unique circuits is strictly smaller.
quotes: In general, the diagonal shift rule for the Hessian is significantly less efficient than the repeated execution of the general parameter-shift rule if the shot count is the relevant resource measure.
to the number of unique circuits, which is strictly smaller for the diagonal shift rule.
assertions.certainty_reason: A comparison under the constant-variance assumption; the shot formulas (Eqs. 40-43) are garbled in the text layer.

assertions.value: The paper states that the Fubini-Study metric tensor can be computed with the same method as the Hessian, using the overlap function f(x) as the cost function, and that the natural gradient requires more circuit evaluations than the Hessian and gradient together.
quotes: It follows that we can compute the metric using the same method as for the Hessian, with f (x) as the cost function.
requires more circuit evaluations than its Hessian and gradient together.
assertions.certainty_reason: A derived statement whose conditions are in the section, not these quotes.

assertions.value: The authors state that the metric tensor depends solely on the ansatz and not on the observable, so for a multi-term cost function it needs computing once per epoch rather than once per term, and an epoch of quantum natural gradient descent can then be cheaper than an epoch of optimizers using the Hessian.
quotes: it depends solely on the ansatz, and not the observable being measured.
the metric only needs to be computed once per epoch, rather than once per term, as is the case of the cost function Hessian.
assertions.certainty_reason: A claim made in discussion of resource counts, without a measurement.

assertions.value: The authors state that the covariance-based block-diagonal method is the best choice for the block-diagonal of the metric, and that using it as an approximation to the full metric has been shown to work well for some circuit structures but not for others.
quotes: making this method the best choice for the block-diagonal.
the approximation has been shown to work well for some circuit structures [48], but not for others [59]
assertions.certainty_reason: The approximation result is attributed to Refs. [48] and [59].

assertions.value: The authors state that knowing all frequencies of the QAOA cost function requires the full spectrum of the problem Hamiltonian, in particular its largest eigenvalue, which is the solution of MaxCut itself, so the motivation for performing QAOA would become obsolete; in general one must instead use upper bounds, and not all integers up to the largest eigenvalue need be present, so the estimate of R may be too large.
quotes: Note that knowing all frequencies of E(x) requires knowledge of the full spectrum of HP
which in turn is the solution of MaxCut itself.
As a consequence, the motivation for performing QAOA becomes obsolete.
not all integers smaller than λ need to be present in the set of frequencies
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own statement of a limit on applying the rule to QAOA, Section 5.1.

assertions.value: The paper states that the QAOA mixing layer, treated as a single operation, makes the cost an N-order trigonometric polynomial in its parameter so the shift rules apply with R = N, and that the problem layer obeys the shift rule for R = M (M the number of edges), although better upper bounds on R may be given.
quotes: E(x) can be considered an N -order trigonometric polynomial in x2j, and the parameter-shift rules we derive in Sec. 3 will apply with R = N .
it will obey the parameter-shift rule for R = M , although we may be able to give better upper bounds λ for R.
assertions.certainty_reason: The statement is quoted but its derivation conditions (eigenvalues of the mixing Hamiltonian) are garbled in the text layer.

assertions.value: The authors report that, for MaxCut QAOA, the number of evaluations for the gradient is cut in half, and those for the gradient and Hessian together scale with halved order in N (and k for regular graphs), where the generalized rule uses an upper bound on the largest eigenvalue and the improved Hessian scheme.
quotes: We systematically observe the number of evaluations for the gradient to be cut in half, and the those for the gradient and Hessian together to scale with halved order in N (and k, for regular graphs).
assertions.certainty_reason: A scaling comparison from the paper's own table for the MaxCut QAOA case.

assertions.value: The authors report, from sampled random unweighted graphs, that both SDP-based upper bounds gave an exact estimate of the largest eigenvalue in the regime N at most 20, as shown by Goemans-Williamson cut values that coincide with the upper bound, and that for all graph types but complete graphs the SDP-based bounds give a better estimate of the number of terms than the analytic bound.
quotes: For this, we sampled random unweighted graphs of the corresponding type and size and ran the GW algorithm as well as an improvement thereof to obtain tighter bounds [71].
we find both SDP-based upper bounds to provide an exact estimate of the largest eigenvalue in the N ≤ 20 regime
For all graph types but complete graphs, the SDP-based upper bounds yield a better estimate for the number of terms than the respective analytic bound φ
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one numerical study on sampled graphs.
assertions.reader_inference: The exactness claim covers only the small sizes tested; the paper does not claim it beyond that regime.

assertions.value: The paper reports evaluation numbers for the gradient and for gradient plus Hessian for QAOA circuits with n = 6 parameters for MaxCut on several graph types and sizes, comparing a decomposition-based method with the new shift rule and analytic or numerical upper bounds.
quotes: Evaluation numbers Neval for the gradient (left) or both the gradient and the Hessian (right) for n = 6 parameter QAOA circuits for MaxCut on graphs of several types and sizes.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own statement of the setup of its numerical comparison, Fig. 3 caption.

assertions.value: The authors state that for certain graph types knowledge of the spectrum's structure and tight analytic bounds already give the advantage, whereas for other graph types the SDP-based bounds reduce the evaluation numbers significantly.
quotes: For certain graph types, knowledge about the structure of the spectrum and tight analytic bounds provide this advantage already, whereas for other graph types the SDP-based bounds reduce the evaluation numbers significantly.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical summary from one numerical study.

assertions.value: The paper states, as a cited property of the Goemans-Williamson SDP relaxation, that the largest eigenvalue is guaranteed to be within a factor of about 0.878 of these SDP upper bounds.
quotes: The largest eigenvalue is guaranteed to be within ∼ 0.878 of these SDP upper bounds.
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the paper takes from the Goemans-Williamson literature (Ref. [70]).

assertions.value: The paper states that Rotosolve reconstructs the cost function in one parameter at a time using 2Rk +1 evaluations, and that the cost reduction for the gradient stems from a cost reduction for function reconstruction and hence applies to Rotosolve as well.
quotes: the cost function is reconstructed as a function of that parameter using 2Rk +1 evaluations
our cost reduction for the gradient presented in Sec. 5.1 stems from a cost reduction for function reconstruction, and hence is applicable to Rotosolve as well.
assertions.certainty_reason: A statement of consequences; no Rotosolve run is reported in the paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that the work extends their generalization of Rotosolve beyond the previously known integer-frequency case, although the number of frequencies, and thus the cost, is typically significantly increased for noninteger frequencies.
quotes: This extends our generalization of Rotosolve beyond the previously known integer-frequency case [42, 45]
typically significantly increased for noninteger frequencies.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states the cost limit of the extension in Section 5.2.

assertions.value: The authors state that, for non-Pauli gates, the minimum of the reconstruction need not have a closed form but the one-dimensional minimization can efficiently be carried out numerically to high precision, via grid search or semi-definite programming.
quotes: the one-dimensional minimization can efficiently be carried out numerically to high precision, via grid search or semi-definite programming
assertions.certainty_reason: A claim without a run in this paper.

assertions.value: The paper states that recent studies have shown coordinate descent methods to work well on many tasks, although there are limited cases where these methods fail.
quotes: Recent studies have shown such coordinate descent methods to work well on many tasks [73, 50, 45, 74], although there are limited cases where these methods fail [75].
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the paper attributes to other work.

assertions.value: The paper states that quantum analytic descent (QAD) was developed for circuits that exclusively contain Pauli rotations as parametrized gates, and that the algorithm evaluates the cost function at 2n2 + n + 1 points around a reference point (n squared, printed flat).
quotes: QAD has been developed for circuits that exclusively contain Pauli rotations as parametrized gates.
The algorithm evaluates the cost function E at 2n2 + n + 1 points around a reference point x0
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the paper attributes to Ref. [49].

assertions.value: The authors state that, for Pauli rotations only, their first modification of QAD reduces the number of evaluations from 2n2 + n + 1 to (3n2 + n)/2 + 1 (n squared, printed flat), by using the reduced Hessian cost.
quotes: this reduces the number of evaluations from 2n2 + n + 1 to (3n2 + n)/2 + 1.
assertions.certainty_reason: A counting statement; the paper reports no run of the modified QAD.

assertions.value: The paper states that the extended QAD model has 2n2 + 1 degrees of freedom, matching the number of evaluations exactly (n squared, printed flat), and that for Rk = 1 for all k the trigonometric interpolation gives 2n2 + 1 evaluations and model parameters, so it generalizes the extended QAD model.
quotes: This extended model has 2n2 +1 degrees of freedom, which matches the number of evaluations exactly.
Indeed, for Rk = 1 for all k we get back 2(n2 − n + n) + 1 = 2n2 + 1 evaluations and model parameters.
assertions.certainty_reason: Counting statements; the general interpolation count formula is garbled in the text layer.

assertions.value: The authors state that it remains to investigate whether and for which applications the extended QAD model yields a better optimization behaviour, and they demonstrate the qualitative difference between the QAD model, its extension and the multi-frequency generalization on toy circuits and Hamiltonians.
quotes: It remains to investigate whether and for which applications the extension yields a better optimization behaviour
Using toy model circuits and Hamiltonians, we demonstrate the qualitative difference between the QAD model, its extension
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states the open question and the toy scope of its demonstration, Section 5.3.

assertions.value: The paper states that for arbitrary frequencies equidistant shift angles no longer make the DFT uniform, the explicit shift rules for equidistant frequencies do not apply, and in general no closed-form expression for the DFT or the shift rules is known.
quotes: However, choosing equidistant shift angles {xμ} will no longer make the DFT uniform, as was the case for equidistant frequencies.
in general we do not know a closed-form expression for the DFT or the parametershift rules.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own statement of a limit of its closed-form rules, App. B.1.

assertions.value: The authors state that for arbitrary frequencies the odd part and odd-order derivatives still cost 2R evaluations of E, but the even part may no longer be periodic, so evaluating it at pi may require two evaluations, leading to 2R + 1 evaluations overall.
quotes: the odd part and thus odd-order derivatives can be obtained at the same price of 2R evaluations of E as before
actually may require two evaluations of E, leading to 2R + 1 evaluations overall.
assertions.certainty_reason: A counting result with its condition (non-periodic even part) stated in App. B.1.

assertions.value: The paper states that for a decomposition with the argument x rescaled individually in each elementary gate, R in general equals P squared (printed P2), which makes the decomposition-based parameter-shift rule beneficial.
quotes: in general will result in R = P2 frequencies of E, making the decompositionbased parameter-shift rule beneficial.
assertions.certainty_reason: The form of the decomposition (Eq. 93) is garbled in the text layer, so the condition is not quoted.

assertions.value: The authors state that for non-equidistant frequencies the Hessian off-diagonal entry may require up to 2Rkm + 1 = 4RkRm + 2Rk + 2Rm − 3 evaluations, which makes the general rule more expensive than decomposition if Rk is not small relative to Pk, and that the same growth for the metric tensor makes the decomposition-based shift rule more feasible for non-equidistant frequencies.
quotes: this may require up to 2Rkm + 1 = 4RkRm + 2Rk + 2Rm − 3 evaluations (see App. A.2)
making the decomposition-based shift rule more feasible for unitaries with non-equidistant frequencies.
assertions.certainty_reason: A counting bound with its condition (arbitrary frequencies) quoted from App. B.2.
assertions.reader_inference: The text layer lost the comparison sign between Rk and Pk, so the exact condition is not stated in the value.

assertions.value: The paper states that the generalization in Ref. [52] is obtained by decomposing the gate generator using Cartan subalgebras, which can yield fewer shifted evaluations than decompositions of the gate itself.
quotes: The generalization of the parametershift rule in Ref. [52] is obtained by decomposing the gate generator using Cartan subalgebras, which can yield fewer shifted evaluations than decompositions of the gate itself.
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the paper attributes to other work.

assertions.value: The paper states that in Ref. [42] the functions of variational quantum algorithms were considered as Fourier series and parameter-shift rules were derived, and that Refs. [42, 45] also proposed a generalized Rotosolve algorithm prior to its eponymous paper.
quotes: In Ref. [42], the functions of VQAs were considered as Fourier series and parameter-shift rules were derived.
Refs. [42, 45] also propose a generalized Rotosolve algorithm prior to its eponymous paper.
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the paper attributes to other work.

assertions.value: The authors state that the two-term parameter-shift rule is restricted to gates with two distinct eigenvalues, potentially requiring expensive decompositions to compute hardware-compatible quantum gradients, and that known extensions remain restricted to gates with a particular number of distinct eigenvalues.
quotes: this twoterm parameter-shift rule is restricted to gates with two distinct eigenvalues
they remain restricted to gates with a particular number of distinct eigenvalues
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own statement of the limit of the prior rule that motivates the work.

assertions.value: The paper states that the original parameter-shift rule gives the derivative for functions with a single frequency (a generator with two eigenvalues), and that a second-order derivative can be had from two function evaluations, valid for single-frequency gates.
quotes: The shift can be chosen smartly so that two function evaluations suffice to obtain the second-order derivative
which like Eq. (7) is valid for single-frequency gates.
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the paper attributes to other work (Ref. [46]).

assertions.value: The authors state that the equidistant frequency case has two major advantages over the general case: closed-form parameter-shift rules can be derived, and the number of circuits required for the rule scales much better; they restrict to integer frequencies without loss of generality by rescaling.
quotes: The equidistant frequency case has two major advantages over the general case
Without loss of generality, we further restrict the frequencies to integer values
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own statement of the scope of Sections 3 and 4.

assertions.value: The paper states that the position zero for the derivative is chosen for convenience and that the shift rule can be applied at any position.
quotes: The position 0 for the derivative is chosen for convenience but the rule can be applied at any position.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own statement of the scope of its rules; the footnote gives the reason (shifting the argument does not change the functional form).

assertions.value: The authors state that they are not aware of a prior reference for the derivations of the odd-part and even-part reconstructions, and that for the odd part a closed-form formula for the derivative at zero can be extracted because it only depends on the odd part of E.
quotes: we are not aware of a prior reference for the derivations for this subsection (reconstructing the odd part) and the next (reconstructing the even part)
We also can extract from here a closed-form formula for the derivative at x = 0, as it only depends on the odd part of E.
assertions.certainty_reason: A novelty statement by the authors, not a result.

assertions.value: The authors list open questions: whether better bounds on the number of frequencies can be had in other situations, whether an approximate or stochastic parameter-shift rule can scale better than the naive method for a general generator, whether truncating the rules to smaller frequencies makes sense, whether there is a classification of problems on which Rotosolve and QAD work well, and whether Fourier analysis can improve optimization in the presence of noise.
quotes: In which situations can we obtain better bounds on the number of frequencies?
Can we apply an approximate or stochastic parameter-shift rule with a better scaling?
Would it ever make sense to truncate these parameter-shift rules to keep only terms corresponding to smaller frequencies?
Is there a classification of problems on which these model-based algorithms work well?

The first copy was read in full; the second was not needed. The file name carries the 2023 arXiv title (Complexity analysis of weakly noisy quantum states via quantum machine learning); the text is the later retitled version of the same arXiv id 2303.17813.
papers.what_it_is: A conference paper that gives a classical-shadow-based learning algorithm that predicts a limited-structure circuit complexity of weakly noisy quantum states, with stated sample and running-time bounds and small simulations.

existing.note: The theorem on efficiency holds for noisy depth of order log n, for the structured complexity prediction task (which has an indeterminate case), and for an ideal learner device. The sample lower bound theorem is proved for a different task (Task 2 in Appendix J: telling apart the outputs of two noisy circuits of different depth), not for the prediction task, and it grows only linearly in the noisy depth. The body calls the algorithm nearly optimal in the depth; only the abstract says optimal. The upper bound on samples is stated without a derivation in the paper.
existing.value: The paper states that, for poly(n) copies of a weakly noisy state of depth R = O(log n) and a particular architecture A, a learning algorithm of poly(n, R, 1/ε) quantum and classical cost solves the structured complexity prediction problem SCP(A, ε), and that the sample complexity lower bound may grow linearly with the circuit layer, so that the algorithm is nearly optimal in the circuit depth; the abstract calls the algorithm optimal in sample complexity with polynomial classical processing time.

quotes: Given poly(n) copies of an n-qubit unknown weakly noisy state ρun that is generated by a noisy quantum device with depth R ̃ = O(log n) (Def. 2)
and a particular architecture A, there exists a poly(n, R ̃, 1/ε) quantum and classical cost learning algorithm which can efficiently solve the SCP(A, ε) problem.
This implies the sample complexity lower bound may linearly growth with the increasing of the circuit layer R ̃, and our learning algorithm is nearly-optimal in terms of the circuit depth
Our algorithm is proved to be optimal in terms of sample complexity accompanied with polynomial classical processing time.

So the word optimal rests on the depth dependence only; the reader did not find a tight bound in n.

assertions.value: The paper defines the task SCP(A, ε): given an architecture A, a weakly noisy n-qubit state and an approximation error ε, design a learning algorithm QLn that runs on an ideal quantum device with polynomially many qubits in n, that returns True if an integer x < log n lies in UDI(ε) (completeness), False if log n ∈ LDI(ε) (soundness), and either answer arbitrarily if all integers in [0, log n] lie outside both intervals (indeterminate case).
quotes: design a learning algorithm QLn that runs on an ideal quantum device with polynomially many qubits in n
1. (Completeness) If there exists an integer x < log n such that x ∈ UDI(ε), then QLn returns True.
2. (Soundness) If log n ∈ LDI(ε), then QLn returns False.
3. (Indeterminate case) If all integers x ∈ [0, log n] lie in UDIc(ε) ∪ LDIc(ε), then QLn may return either True or False arbitrarily.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own task definition.

assertions.value: The paper defines the upper decision interval UDI(ε) as the integer interval [u, ∞) on which max LR(β) ≤ ε holds and the lower decision interval LDI(ε) as the integer interval [0, l] on which min LR(β) ≥ 2ε holds.
quotes: Definition 4 (Decision interval) UDI(ε) is defined as the integer interval [u, ∞) such that for any R ∈ UDI(ε), it holds that maxβ⃗ LR β⃗ ≤ ε.
Similarly, LDI(ε) is defined as the integer interval [0, l] such that for any R ∈ LDI(ε), we have minβ⃗ LR β⃗ ≥ 2ε.

assertions.value: The paper defines the property DP(A, ε): a weakly noisy state has it if it can be distinguished from the maximally mixed state with bias at least the quoted threshold by an R-depth (R < log n) measurement U|0n⟩⟨0n|U† with U from the architecture class; the algorithm returns True (False) to indicate that the state does (does not) have it.
quotes: Definition 5 (Distinguishable Property, DP(A, ε)) We say an n-qubit weakly noisy quantum state ρun satisfies DP(A, ε) if ρun can be distinguished from In/2n with the bias at least 1 − 2−n − ε by using a R-depth (R < log n) QCA measurement MQCA = U |0n⟩⟨0n|U †, where U ∈ UA.
We note that the learning algorithm QLn returns True (respectively, False) to indicate that ρun does (does not) satisfy the DP(A, ε) property.

papers.what_it_is: A theory paper that proposes a quantum natural policy gradient algorithm with a classical outer loop and a quantum inner loop, and proves a sample complexity of order epsilon to the power minus 1.5 in a quantum-oracle model of an infinite-horizon discounted MDP.

existing.note: Theorem 3 (Sec. 4.3) carries conditions the stored value does not. It needs Assumptions 1 to 3, learning parameters set by Lemmas 3 and 6, sufficiently small epsilon, and the listed choices of H, N, K and the target variances. The guarantee is an optimality gap of at most the square root of epsilon-bias plus epsilon, not epsilon alone. The Abstract's 'classical lower bound' is the classical rate that the paper cites as the established optimal sample complexity (Mondal and Aggarwal, 2024a); the paper proves no lower bound itself.
existing.value: The authors state in Theorem 3 that, when Assumptions 1 to 3 hold, the learning parameters are chosen as in Lemma 3 and Lemma 6, epsilon is sufficiently small, H and N are of order log of one over epsilon, K is of order one over epsilon, the gradient target variance is of order epsilon and the Fisher target variance is of order the fourth power of one minus gamma times epsilon, then the average optimality gap is at most the square root of epsilon-bias plus epsilon. The authors state that this gives a sample complexity of order epsilon to the power minus 1.5, counted as queries to the quantum oracle, and an iteration complexity of order epsilon to the power minus 1.

assertions.reader_inference: The paper cites Jerbi et al. (2023), Quantum policy gradient algorithms, and Wang et al. (2021a), a tabular model-free setting. Whether those cover the same ground is not tested in this paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that most existing work in quantum reinforcement learning is limited to the tabular setup and that the results do not directly extend to large state spaces with a parameterized policy. They claim theirs is the first work to address infinite horizon MDPs with general parameterized policies.
quotes: most existing works are still limited to the tabular setup.
However, the results don't directly extend to large state spaces, where a parameterized policy is used.
To the best of our knowledge, ours is the first work to address infinite horizon MDPs with general parameterized policies.
assertions.certainty_reason: A priority claim and a literature summary by the authors.

assertions.value: The authors state that the paper addresses the trade-off between bias and unbiased estimation, that the deterministic approach introduces a bounded bias, and that it achieves orders reduction in sample complexity compared with its classical counterparts. They state that unlike classical algorithms, quantum methods rely on deterministic operations, which complicates the design of unbiased estimators.
quotes: Unlike classical algorithms, quantum methods rely on deterministic operations, complicating the design of unbiased estimators for policy gradients.
While this approach introduces a bounded bias, it achieves orders reduction in sample complexity compared to its classical counterparts.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author claim in the introduction; the quantified result is Theorem 3.
assertions.reader_inference: The phrase 'orders reduction' is not quantified in the paper; Theorem 3 gives a polynomial improvement from epsilon to the power minus 2 to epsilon to the power minus 1.5 in the stated oracle model.

assertions.value: The authors state that stochastic cutting-plane methods were proposed by Sidford and Zhang (2024) to achieve better sample complexity, that extending them to reinforcement learning would require an entirely new algorithmic framework because of the non-convex nature of RL with general parameterization, and that the techniques of Agarwal et al. for moving from local to global convergence do not apply, preventing similar guarantees.
quotes: To achieve better sample complexity guarantees, stochastic cutting-plane methods have been proposed in (Sidford & Zhang, 2024).
Extending these methods to RL, however, would require an entirely new algorithmic framework.
preventing similar guarantees for such methods in RL.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state a limit on what their approach and its relatives can do, in Section 1.1.
assertions.reader_inference: This is the authors' stated reason that the rate stops at epsilon to the power minus 1.5; it is not proved.

assertions.value: The authors state that their study focuses on policy gradient methods and that quantum actor-critic algorithms remain largely unexplored, and that classical results offer order-optimal sample complexity guarantees for actor-critic, which makes the search for quantum speedups there a key open direction. They state that extending the constrained setup of Mondal and Aggarwal (2024b) to the quantum setting is another open direction.
quotes: While our study focuses on policy gradient methods, quantum actor–critic algorithms remain largely unexplored.
making the search for quantum speedups in this setting a key open direction.
Another open direction is extending the constrained setup studied in (Mondal & Aggarwal, 2024b) to the quantum setting.
assertions.certainty_reason: Limits and open problems in the paper's Conclusion.

assertions.value: The authors conclude that the QNPG algorithm uses quantum mean estimation and a deterministic gradient sampling approach, adapts the classical sampling method into a quantum-compatible deterministic procedure, and achieves a sample complexity of order epsilon to the power minus 1.5 improving on the classical state-of-the-art of order epsilon to the power minus 2. They state that the algorithm balances the trade-off between deterministic encoding and bounded bias.
quotes: we achieve a sample complexity of O ̃(ε−1.5), improving upon the O ̃(ε−2) result of the classical state-of-the-art result.
The algorithm balances the trade-off between deterministic encoding and bounded bias,
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' summary of their own result.
assertions.reader_inference: Here the classical rate is called a state-of-the-art result, while the Abstract and Section 1.2 call it a lower bound.

papers.title_in_file: Entangled Mixed-State Datasets Generation by Quantum Machine Learning
papers.version_note: arXiv:2503.06452v1 [quant-ph] 9 Mar 2025. The text layer holds the paper twice (preprint copy twice in sequence); the first copy was read and the second used only to check quotes. The text layer has no page breaks, so the page count is an estimate.
papers.what_it_is: A QML paper that generates entangled mixed-state datasets with concentratable-entanglement lower bounds and benchmarks three ansatz families on entangled-separable classification for 2 to 5 qubits.

The coordinator should check the PDF. If a CEL above zero is also reached by separable states, a target CEL of 0.25 does not by itself certify an entangled state (the paper gives no independent check).

assertions.value: The authors state that a mixed state can be obtained in a circuit by tracing out an ancillary register of an entangled pure state, citing the purification theorem of Ref. [49], and call this a form of anti-purification.
quotes: According to the purification theorem in Ref. [49]
the method of obtaining mixed states in a quantum circuit is actually a form of anti-purification
assertions.certainty_reason: A cited theorem used as the design basis.

assertions.value: The paper tests three ansatz families for generating mixed states: the hardware-efficient ansatz (HWE, Ref. [52]), the strongly-entangling ansatz (SEA, Ref. [53]) and the simplified 2-design ansatz (SD, Ref. [54]).
quotes: Hardware-efficient ansatz (HWE)[52] in Fig. 3(a): Composed of layers of single-qubit rotations denoted by R and entangled layers
Strongly-entangling ansatz (SEA)[53] in Fig. 3(b): Composed of arbitrary single-qubit rotations denoted by R and varied pattern CNOT entanglement
Simplified 2-design ansatz (SD)[54] in Fig. 3(c):Composed of PauliY rotations denoted by Ry and entanglers bwtween neighbor qubits
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 3.2 defines the three ansatz.

assertions.value: The authors state that for each ansatz they varied depth l (1 to 4) and width w (2 to 5) and randomly generated 100 states per circuit, to see the purity distributions.
quotes: For each type, we considered different depth (denoted by l, with l = 1, 2, 3, 4) and width (denoted by w, with w = 2, 3, 4, 5).
For all circuits, we randomly generated 100 states
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 3.2 states the setup.

assertions.value: The authors report from the purity distributions that SEA is notably susceptible to depth and width, the SD purity shifts lower as depth and width grow, and the HWE purity stays largely invariant with width; they conclude all three can generate mixed states.
quotes: The SEA(the green area) is notably susceptible to variations in both depth and width.
As both depth and width increase, the distribution of purity for the SD(the orange area) shifts towards lower values.
The HWE(the blue area) , however, remains largely invariant with respect to variations in width.
types of ansatz are all affected by depth and width, yet they are all capable of generating mixed states.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study.

assertions.value: The authors conclude from the continuity bound and unitary invariance that when the initial states are sufficiently close, the CELs of the states after a unitary are also close.
quotes: Therefore, based on the unitary invariance, we can conclude that when the initial states are sufficiently close, the CELs of two quantum states after the action of a unitary operator are also close.
assertions.certainty_reason: A consequence stated without its own proof.
assertions.reader_inference: It follows if the trace distance is unitarily invariant (a standard fact the paper does not state).

assertions.value: The paper's generation method: prepare a mixed state with a desired CEL value, perturb it with local transformations to get an initial set P, and train a parameterized circuit so the CEL of each output is within a tolerance delta of a target value xi.
quotes: So, we could firstly generate an mixed state ρin with an desired CEL value.
By applying different perturbations ε to the initial state through local transformations, we can obtain an initial state dataset P
we just need to train the parameters such that |Cσl (S)−ξ| ≤ δ, where σ = U (θ)ρinU †(θ) and δ is the tolerant value.

with the rotation angles randomly selected from the interval (−ε, ε).

assertions.certainty_reason: An author conclusion; the only support is the single Fig. 5 run.

assertions.value: The paper states that it built four datasets of 2, 3, 4 and 5 qubits; the entangled part of each holds 6,000 states from SD, HWE and SEA, made with epsilon 0.5 and target CEL 0.25, and the separable part holds 6000 states.

We set ε = 0.5 and ξ = 0.25 in construction entangled mixed-state datasets.
it contains a total of 6,000 quantum states generated by SD, HWE, and SEA, respectively, with different numbers of layers

The paper labels a state entangled by its target CEL, and Sec. 3.1 reports CEL above zero for separable states, so the entangled labels are not independently certified in the text.

To avoid entanglement, only random controlled rotation gates are implemented between ancillary register and target register.
the control qubit is randomly chosen from the ancillary register, and the target qubit from the target register.

for the n-qubit datasets, where n = 2, 3, 4, 5, the range of circuit widths is {n, n + 1, n + 2, n + 3}}, while the depth is independent of n and the range of depths is {3, 4, 5, 6}.
with a batch size of 32 used in our experiments

with the final stable success rate increasing with the system size.

deeper models achieving higher accuracy and F1 Score as the system size increases.
Therefore, we conclude that in this work, the depth of the ansatz plays a primary role in its learning performance.

While the SEA and the HWE demonstrate more stable performance.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study.

quotes: Using SD for related work may increase additional debugging workload.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author remark without evidence in the paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that by the cyclic property of the trace the measured value of the circuit on a state equals the trace of the state with a rotated observable, so the circuit can be read as acting on the observable, and tie this to entanglement witnesses.
assertions.anchor: Section 4, after the GHZ and W result
quotes: the measurement outcome Tr(U (θ)ρiU †(θ)O) can be equivalently expressed as Tr(ρO(θ)), where O(θ) = U †(θ)OU (θ).
This implies that U (θ) can also be interpreted as acting on the observable O.
assertions.certainty_reason: A standard identity stated without a proof; the link to witnesses is the authors' argument.

assertions.value: The authors claim that supervised QML could supersede entanglement witnesses when supported by high-quality quantum datasets.
quotes: This discovery shows that supervised QML could supersede entanglement witnesses when supported by high-quality quantum datasets.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author claim; no experiment in the paper tests it.
assertions.reader_inference: It sits beside the paper's own statements that GHZ and W learning reached only 60% and that witnesses should still be combined with high accuracy.

assertions.value: The authors state that supervised QML can classify two state sets when a supporting hyperplane exists between their convex hulls and cannot when none exists, giving Werner-state classification as an example where it is unsuitable without other optimizations.
quotes: When there exists a supporting hyperplane between the convex hulls of two state sets in the state space, supervised QML can effectively accomplish the task.
When there is no supporting hyperplane between the convex hulls of two quantum state sets, supervised QML cannot perform effective classification[44, 45].
For example, without the aid of other algorithmic optimizations, supervised QML is not suitable for entanglement-separability classification of the Werner states.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author claim with citations; no proof in the paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that even when accuracy is high, entanglement witnesses should be combined for analysis, otherwise the learning motivation cannot be explained, and leave this for future research.
quotes: Even when the accuracy is high, entanglement witnesses should be combined for analysis; otherwise, the learning motivation cannot be explained.
We will not further discuss such work in this paper but leave it for future research.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 4 states this limit.

assertions.value: The authors state open problems: more accurate and computationally feasible entanglement measures than CEL, scalability to more qubits, and decoherence and gate errors before generation on real quantum hardware.
quotes: Although the CEL provides a useful tool, more accurate and computationally feasible measures are still required to enhance the quality of the dataset.
Second, the scalability of our approach to larger systems (more qubits) needs to be explored.
Practical limitations, such as decoherence and gate errors, must be addressed to ensure the feasibility of generating entangled states on real quantum hardware.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section 5 states these limits.
assertions.reader_inference: Every result in the paper is from numerical simulation of at most 5 qubits in the data sets.

assertions.value: The authors conclude that their approach provides a valuable resource for benchmarking QML models and opens new avenues for exploring entanglement in mixed states.
quotes: Our approach not only provides a valuable resource for benchmarking QML models but also opens new avenues for exploring the rich structure of quantum entanglement in mixed states.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author conclusion.

assertions.certainty_reason: An author claim; Section 5 lists scalability as untested.
assertions.reader_inference: Section 5 says scalability to more qubits still needs to be explored.

quantum NFL theorem demonstrated that the effect of quantum entangled datasets on prediction error exhibits a double effect, depending critically on the number of measurements allowed.

the field of quantum machine learning still suffers from an absence of comprehensive, large-scale quantum datasets
